translations.text: I marveled with you, O lovers of Christ, because the new grace of the Gospel was proclaimed through the Old Testament.
My mind was enlightened with yours, because I saw the apostolic writings illuminated by the words of the prophets. I acknowledge the grace so that I may receive the reward.
I saw the new mystery preached by the old, when Abraham gave an oath to his servant upon his thigh;
he had him put his hand under his thigh, and called the God of heaven and earth to witness the words.
"Put," he says, "your hand under my thigh, and I will make you swear by the Lord God, maker of heaven and earth." There is a great question in this saying,
for it was set down on account of the offspring that was to come forth from the thigh of Jacob, according to the saying, "A ruler shall not fail from Judah,

nor a leader from his thighs." How then is the oath found to be sworn by the Life-giver? For Isaac had been born long before, and the offspring had already sprung forth; and when he gave the oath there was no hope of any other offspring from the thigh of the blessed man. It is clear that Abraham had in himself the life-giving seed,
about which Paul said that the promises were given to Abraham and to his seed; and examining the matter, he explains it in the Epistle to the Galatians:
"It was not said," he says, "'to you and to your seeds,' as of many, but 'to you and to your seed,' which is Christ."
It was thus shown that Christ is Abraham’s offspring according to the flesh, and he rightly administered the oath by that offspring.
The question concerning this is how he administered the oath at his loins, since the life-giving flower had already blossomed from him.
For the member had once become an instrument of holiness, and the divine offspring had once dwelt there. For this reason he administered the oath by the temple.
“And whoever swears,” he says, “by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it.” As the Life-giver also said concerning the Pharisees:
“Woe to you, blind Pharisees, because you say that whoever swears by the temple is not bound by anything, but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.
Fools and blind men! Which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? For this reason I tell you: whoever has sworn by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it.”
Just as a royal house that has been the king’s dwelling once and [?], even if the king moves away from it, is called royal because it was once dedicated as a royal residence,
so also the patriarch’s member, which had once become an instrument of the coming dispensation, was a temple of the promised goodness.
And the oath was not in vain, but was a true testimony. Thus he administers the oath by the offspring and explains who the offspring is.
"Put," he says, "your hand under my thigh, and I will give you an oath by the Lord God, maker of heaven and earth." If that is so, Christ our Savior is Lord and God of heaven and earth.
For the same reason, when various revelations appeared to the holy prophet Zechariah, there was a particular revelation of this kind.
“I lifted up,” he says, “my eyes and looked, and behold, a lampstand of cast gold, and seven lamps upon the lampstand,
and seven openings for the lamps, and seven burning globes, and two olive branches on the right and on the left.”
And I said to the angel who was speaking to me, “Lord, what is this?” For what appeared to the eyes was of one kind, while the interpretation to come was of another kind.
The things that appeared did not signify themselves, but foretold certain other things. The prophet asks, “Lord,” he says, “what might this be?”

If he was asking about what was visible, then he was not asking well, if he did not know even so much as what the lampstand was and what the olive trees were. Rather, the prophet seeks to grasp not the visible things but their interpretations. For indeed he says, "What are these?" And the angel says to him:
“Do you not know what this is?” And he says, “No, lord.” With a humble mind he admits his ignorance and learns from the truth.
He too was a brother of the eunuch who heard Philip ask, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
And with a humble mind he says, “How can I understand unless someone guides me?” Likewise, here he says, “Do you not know what this is?” And he says, “No, lord.”
“What are the two olive branches that are on the right and left of the lampstand?” And he explained the olive branches and, along with them, what the lampstand was.
Pay close attention. The lampstand stood in the middle, and the branches were on either side of the lampstand.
But the angel explains that the branches stood not beside the lampstand, but before God, as though the lampstand were a representation of God—or rather, of our Savior and his work in the flesh.

"Do you not know," he says, "what these are?" And he says, "No, lord." "These two branches are the two sons of fatness, who stand before the Lord God of all the earth." One must also attend to that steadfastly:
he calls the lampstand seven-lamped because of the Lord's bodily dispensation.
Indeed, the lampstand itself was the Lord’s body, and it received the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit as an example for us, not because of any need of its own.
As Isaiah also says, "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall blossom from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him." Which Spirit?

Manifold in parts according to the effects it works, and a gift without parts according to its nature. "And the Spirit of God shall rest upon him": the first he says of the essence of the Holy Spirit, for he also calls it the Spirit of God; and in what follows he gives the name "spirit" to the effects that it works in others.
“The spirit,” he says, “of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and reverence for God.”
He speaks of the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit that rested upon the Lord’s body.
The six-branched lampstand also depicts this. A lampstand is shown to make clear the illumination brought about by the workings of the Holy Spirit.
To make this still more certain, a little further down he says, “These are the (seven) eyes of the Lord that look upon all the earth.”

Do you see that for the enlightenment of the whole earth the seven graces rested, as a figure, upon the Lord's body? And to make it still clearer, the evangelist testifies: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." Since the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High were there from the very beginning of the divine conception, what need was there afterward for the seven operations of the Spirit? This is what the disciples of the heretics slanderously claim: that only after his baptism did he become worthy to receive the operations of the Holy Spirit. And we do not deny that the Spirit came at that time; but as the evangelist himself says, "He on whom you see the Spirit descending and resting upon him, he it is"; "and I saw," he says, "and I testify that this is the Son of God." Do you see that he came for testimony, and not to fill some need?
Note how the Truth interprets itself by itself, and has no need of human thoughts:
"These," he says, "are they who stand before the Lord of all the earth." Zechariah calls the Life-giver Lord of all the earth with respect to his bodily dispensation.
Peter, the head of all the apostles, was speaking with Cornelius:

"We," he says, "know the word that came to pass throughout all Judea," of which it had been said before, "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit." There he says: "the word which God sent to proclaim the good news of peace to the sons of Israel."
He is Lord of all: of those in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld. He is Lord of the visible and the invisible.
John also speaks in agreement with him: “He who came from above is above all.”
But I consider it important to refute the heretics' other objection as well,
for they listen to the apostle's words with an impious mind, as though he received some reward for the cross, namely to be above everyone; as though God exalted him because he endured the sufferings.
They fell sick from this because they neither read the apostle's words correctly nor grasped what the words mean. "He humbled himself," he says, "to the point of death, even death on a cross,
and for that reason God also exalted him and gave him the name
that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bend."
"Do you see," they say, "that he was exalted after the cross? Do you notice that he received the exaltation as a reward for the sufferings?"
For if he was exalted after the cross, why would John the Baptist proclaim, “He who came from above is above all”? He did not say that he would be above all, but that [?], and not that he would be.
The Life-giver himself also said, while speaking with the Jews: "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am." For he is eternal: he was, and he will be.
He is not confessed by you, but we render him the confession that is rightly due.

From now on let Christ’s glory and the Spirit’s exaltation be proclaimed; let the Father’s power also be proclaimed. Let the Only-begotten also be exalted; let the Holy Spirit be glorified and praised.

And let no one suppose that we are breaking any order when we speak first of the Son, then of the Spirit, and then of the Father; or first of the Son and the Father, and then of the Spirit. For there was no order of rank in the immortal nature.

When I say there is no order, I do not mean that there is any disorder. I mean that there is no order in which one surpasses another. In the same way, when God is said to be without form, this does not mean any ugliness. It means that he does not have a bodily form. And when he is called imageless, this is not because he lacks the beauty of an image. He is called imageless because he is incorporeal.
Likewise, when I say that the divine nature is without an order of rank, I do not mean to indicate any disorder, but that there are no ranks there that rival one another.

I spoke first of the Father, not because he is first in any order, but as a picture formed in the mind. For he is the begetter of the Only-begotten and the root of the holy fruit. And since he is eternal light, the offspring of the eternal light is eternal light.
If anyone now, here in this orthodox congregation, dared,
where the right confession of all knowledge is found in full, to call the Son more honored than the Father, would he not be reproached right here among the orthodox?
And now, would he not dare to say to the church, “May Christ and his Father bless you”? Would he not indeed give an impression of disorder, since he did not honor the root first and then the fruit?
If someone said, “May the Son and the Father save you,” would he not indeed seem to be causing some confusion, and would you not be angry that he was disrupting the order?

But such opinions do not belong to the just. When someone looks to the truth, he does what is right and carries off the victory by the apostle's ruling: to mention without distinction first the Son, then the Father, and then the Holy Spirit.
And listen to Paul, the great preacher. He writes to the Thessalonians: “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, sanctify you.”
This does not mean that the Son sanctifies first and the Father afterward.

Rather, Paul's clear and luminous spirit wished to show that there is no such order in the Holy One. The one named second is equal in honor to the one named first, and the third is in no way lessened or dishonored.
For this reason he also brings the names forward, for he knows their undivided nature and their inseparable kingdom.
Let us ask Saint Paul: “Where did you get the grounds for speaking about God in this way, placing the Son before the Father—not in rank or power, but in words?”
And now let us say: “Why did you mention the Son first, and then the Father?” Let Paul answer, acting as his own defender and as the teacher of the church:
“I say nothing on my own authority. Christ establishes such teachings through me.” For he himself also says: “If you wish to seek proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.”
If Christ speaks in me, do not slander the Lord's words, and do not find fault with the faith. Or can you not understand and believe that Christ speaks in me?
Listen to the same Christ when he speaks in his own person, with no one between. For if the names of the Holy Trinity stood in an order of subordination, one would be first in order and power,

one second, and one third. Then the Life-giver would not have called himself the truth. "I am the truth," he says. Otherwise he would have confused the order of the truth. And listen again to the Life-giver: does he not speak first of himself and then of the Father? [?]
"If you keep my commandments (Greek: if anyone keeps)," he says, "I and my Father will come" (and so on).
The heretics regard the Father as belonging to some higher rank, and they regard the Son as the Father's chiliarch, like a king's commander.
So let them now be asked: when royal decrees are being issued, would a chiliarch dare to say, "I and the king will give orders,"
For we must understand what is above us from what is familiar to us. Would a created nature dare to place itself before the uncreated nature,
and count himself together with one beyond comparison, to whom he was not equal because the other ranked so far above him, and say,

...that "I and the Father will come, and will make our abode with him." For by saying "I and the Father" he made the distinction of the names plain, and by "we will come and will make our abode" he proclaimed the common honor of their dignity. So also in another place, when the apostle Philip said [?]:
“Lord, show us your Father, and that is enough for us,” the giver of life answered: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” He gives an answer contrary to the question.

"Was it about you that I asked? Was it about you that I wish to learn? 'Show us,' I say, 'your Father,' and not you." And what does he say to that? "Have I been with you so long a time, and you have not known me?"

If the Son is unlike him, how can the unlike one be known through one unlike him? Or how will you see the greater in the lesser, or the greater honor through the inferior, or the Creator through a servant?
"So long a time," he says, "I have been with you." And he did not say, "My Father is with you," but "I." By my being with you, the Father is with you.
"Have I been with you so long a time, and you have not known me?" He said "you have not known me" well. Philip says, "Show," and the Savior says, "Have you not known me?"
He wanted to show that God is not seen but known. And next he adds [?]:
"Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me? So how can you say, 'Show us your Father'?"
This is instead of saying: "How do you expect to see someone else? For if I am in the Father and the Father is in me, and the Son is known through the Father and the Father through the Son,
how can you say, 'Show us your Father,' as if he were someone else? Do you want to leave me aside and see him?"

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”—not as though the nature were somehow mixed together, or as though one cup stood inside another. He is not revealing any bodily connections, but an understanding of thought and word.

“I,” he says, “am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” The Father is not known without the Son, nor is the Son revealed without the Father, just as thought is known through the word, and the word is revealed through thought.
How could I know your thoughts except through the words you speak? Your words reveal your thoughts, and your thoughts give birth to your words.

...and a person's words cannot be understood without the mind, nor the mind without the words that are born from the mind. In the same way the Father is known through the Son, and the Son is revealed through the Father.
For this very reason the evangelist also says, "In the beginning was the Word," so that he might show a birth without passion and explain the unity of essence.
The only-begotten Word, God, is to the Father as the word is to the mind.
These very things are marvelous. I will repeat once more what has been said. Our earlier words concerned this very matter, so that from what belongs to us you might learn what is above us.
While the word is still in the mind, it is invisible within the invisible, intelligible within the intelligible, incorporeal with the incorporeal.

And when the word wishes to come out, it first moves forward into the mouth, and from there it clothes itself with a voice. It does not take its voice from some other nature; rather, speech is articulated from the word itself.
And that which by nature is invisible in its father puts on voice and goes forth. What was formerly unseen becomes plain to all.
And as it goes forward it fills everyone, yet it is not separated from the one who begot it.
Who among human beings, when speaking a word and teaching others, empties himself of that word?
And who would think, “Perhaps, while I put it into another person’s ears, I will leave my own mind naked and stripped bare”?
Did not the word go outside and yet remain there within? Did it not [?] many ears, yet not depart from the one who gave it birth?

Now if a human word, when it proceeds and goes forth out of the mind, is not separated from the one who begot it, would God the Word, who appeared in the world for our sake, have left the Father's bosom empty? Away with it, [?] far be it!
For myriads upon myriads hear the word, and it enters countless ears without being divided. Rather, it is whole with each person, all of it with everyone, and entirely in the mind.

And if the human word is wholly in the mind, and whole with each person, and all of it with everyone, how can they say of the Father that if he begot, then an outflowing and a cutting-off took place, and the indivisible was divided? Let the Life-giver say to them, "Search the Scriptures."
Search them, and do not read idly. Investigate them by putting the depths of their meaning to search and inquiry.

For God set the Scriptures before us but held back the meaning of the oracles. He gave the Scriptures but did not lay bare what is hidden in their interpretations. Instead he left it as an exercise for the courses you run, so that it might train your mental skill, and so that he might see whether you serve the Scriptures or force them.
Just as God first set forth nature and concealed the skill: all materials and substances were set openly before us, while skill arose in human minds. So it is also with the Scriptures.
To make my words still clearer: God set before us the nature of stones, not the building ready-made. He gave wheat; he did not make bread and set it before us.
He gave grapes; he did not himself make the grapes into wine. He gave wool; he did not himself make the garment. He gave gold mixed with earth; he did not himself separate it from [?] the earth. Why?
Because man was made according to the image of God, God shares out the work of creating. He himself makes, and he gives man the skill to fashion the work.
For example, he gave man, who was made in the image of God, a share in assigning names to created beings.

He himself, as Creator, brought them from nonexistence into existence, and commanded his image to give them names. Likewise, he himself provided the materials and entrusted the fashioning of the work to skill.
Who first fashioned a plow to break up the earth with wood and iron and open a furrow, and made a yoke and a drawbar, and harnessed oxen for work with yoke-pins?
Wood and iron existed, but skill was nowhere among them. Who showed you, O man, to say, “I fashioned a plow in this way,” or that the hard substance of iron would soften in fire?
Who showed you how to sit and toil, and out of so great a bulk to make a tiny needle? Who put it into your mind to make door [?] and bolts, or to fit together the beams and roofs of houses?
“You are asking a very foolish question,” he says. “I have God within me as the teacher of skills, and you ask, ‘Where did you learn?’”
And so, brothers, everywhere this human nature of ours, imitating its Lord, adorns natural things through skills.
If it remains within its limits, the image is good; but if it exceeds its limits, it is dishonored by its excess.
Here is an example: man learned to drive the ox, train the horse, tame the camel, and likewise the other animals that were given to serve us.

But out of greed he also devised another kind of mixing, contrary to nature: putting the ass to the mare, which was not according to the will of God. For in the beginning God said, "Let the earth bring forth four-footed beasts and creeping things according to their kind." Greed devised another mixing as well, a mixing contrary to nature.
For this reason God, to punish the excess, made the offspring of human greed barren. That is why the mule does not give birth,

for it is not one of those that, when they came into being, heard: "Increase and multiply and fill the earth." Yet he allows the image to do whatever it wishes, so that he may show its power, punish its excess and expose its pride.

Again, unrestrained desire conceived the making of an image in human form. “Let me imitate God,” it says, “who made the human image, and make an image of the body.” And it forces nature through skill.
And because it heard that God took soil from the earth and made man, skill fell into perplexity, because it could not truly imitate its Lord. It then took refuge in devices and contrivances.
He gathers roots and flowers for colours for [?]. He makes eyes like real eyes, but they do not see.
He measures out ears, but they do not hear. He polishes noses, but they do not smell. He [?] the mouth, but there is no speech on the lips.
He fashions the shape of feet and thighs, but the feet do not walk or take a step. By this he makes it clear that he allowed the image to do whatever it wished, but not to go beyond the measure.
so that he may not become proud and fail to recognize his nature, or the freedom and salvation of his soul.
But since they learned that man was created from the earth, I [?] wish to imitate the Lord and Creator by another art as well:
the art of physicians. When he sees rot in the body, he puts iron to work and cuts the rot away.
And when he wishes to [?] the wound, bring about healing, and restore the wasted flesh to its proper size, he is not a creator who creates it anew.

Now, by what art does the image work to imitate its Lord? He runs to the soil from which the body was created and prepares remedies and plasters from it. With one he removes the rot, with the other he builds up the body, and in this way he makes up what the body lacks.
And see the marvels: how God sits and looks on, as if at children.
And what does his looking show? It is not that he is learning; it is that he is training. In this way the fountain of all good things instructs his image.

As at the beginning, God placed before Adam all the wild animals, livestock, and birds, to see what he would call them—not so that the all-knowing one might learn, but so that he might train his image.
The desire to put [?] into the mind reveals the useful methods of building, carpentry, shipbuilding, metalworking, and weaving.

Also, looking at the stars is not idle work. Observing the order of the stars is useful to sailors: they heed the eastern stars and recognise the right time for an easy voyage. It is not for casting nativities, nor [?] for bringing in myths of lot and fortune.
but to follow the Lord’s words: “Let there be lights in the heavens, and let them shine upon the earth, and let them serve as signs, and for days and seasons.”
So that you may not suppose that the image discovers the means of doing everything on his own, the blessed Solomon makes this clear with a single statement.
“He gave me,” he says, “knowledge of whatever exists: an unerring understanding of the structure of the world and the arrangement of created things, the beginning, end, and middle of times,

"The cycles of the elements and the order of the stars, the habits of animals and the rage of wild beasts, plants of every kind and the powers of roots, whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest, what is seen and what is unseen, I came to know," he says, "I, a man", instead of saying "I, the image". And how? He says:
"Wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me." But it taught you the things that have measure, not the immeasurable.
See how far the craft spread and advanced, beyond measure. It looked at human nature, and the image of God considered how the instrument of the mouth’s speech was formed.
He observed nature, and he imitates nature by art,
and he devises contrivances with many pipes joined and fitted to one another. And see what art does to imitate the work of the Artificer:
it makes bags for me which do not hold breath of their own, but by giving and taking, opening and shutting, borrow outside air,

and then it passes the breath from the two bellows into wind-carrying tubes, and from there into all the pipes. He realises that although the breath plays through them, no melody is produced, so he devises a further contrivance for that: he arranges the notes with his fingers and trills the melodies.
And where did this come from for you, O man? How did you learn to construct bellows that take in air, and to shape the filtered air into melodies with your fingers?
“You ask very foolishly,” he says. “Did I not already say that I am his image? Here I looked at my own nature and imitated it.”

For they see in me an outside breath coming in, and these coverings, by opening and closing often, take in the common air. I see that two passages give and take the air into the mouth, as if through a kind of funnel [?].
I see that the air enters, yet speech does not happen unless the tongue moves between them and shapes the sounds.

I looked within myself and drew a comparison from my own nature, and through my own person I came to understand the Lord’s craftsmanship. As David also says, “Your knowledge has become wonderful in me.”
Here I looked within myself and glorified the craftsman. I became like my Lord, and through craftsmanship I visibly portrayed my nature.
The harp is not something evil; rather, it became an instrument for filthy songs. If it sang divine praises as it did at first, it would not be impure.
Although they are causes of unrestrained desire at feasts, nevertheless, if they were dedicated to God as at first, they would not be evil and impure.
As David also says, “Praise the Lord with the psaltery, with the lyre, with strings, with the harp, and with cymbals, with sweet sounds, with praise, with the tambourine, and with dancing.”
Now, if such a thing were not for dissolute revelry, nor again for the worship of idols,
but if he gave fruit to God by the same means through which he learned the art, the skill of the art would not be blameworthy,
if he knew the Lord. The lyre would not be blameworthy if someone offered songs to God with the lyre.
For this reason, blessed David did not sing filthy songs with the lyre, but offered sacred praises to God and put demons to flight.
When the evil spirit tormented Saul, the Scriptures say that David played the lyre, and Saul found relief.
Do you see that every art has been fashioned for God’s pleasure? There would be no evil if everything were done according to God’s will.

What, then, did I wish to show, that I turned from speaking about God to words like these, about art and about an image resembling its creator? I wished to show that I [?] the Lord's words and refute the baseless opinions of the schismatics. The Lord's? Which words?
“Hypocrites,” he says, “you know how to interpret the appearance of the sky. You know the arts, you have understood wisdom, and yet you insult the craftsman of all things?”

You became like your Lord through your craftsmanship and made whatever you wished, for you were established in the image and likeness of the Creator. Yet do you proclaim that the Creator is unlike the one who begot him?
I freed you who were subject to sins, and do you call me, who am Lord of all, into subjection?
"Yes," they say, "for it is written that the Son shall be subject."

We have already spoken about this as far as we were able, or rather by the power of God, for these words are not ours but God's; remember them. Even so, let us now direct a few more refutations against them.
Let us examine the statement. In the world to come and in the resurrection, where you say that the Son will be subjected, will you not indeed become a sun and an angel?

"In the resurrection of the dead," he says, "men do not take wives, nor do women belong to husbands, but they will be like the angels." Will you then rise above your rank, while the Son comes down from lordship?
Have you not heard from Paul? “Creation,” he says, “was subjected to futility, and creation itself groans and suffers labor pains until now.”
If created things—that is, heaven and earth and everything else—were subjected to humanity’s futility,

For he calls it vanity because the image was corrupted and man sank to the likeness of the beasts. So also elsewhere he says, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity"; and David says, "Every living man is altogether vanity."
So the creatures were made subject to man, who corrupted the image. And how were they made subject?
For the sun rises on the unworthy, rains fall, springs flow for the ungrateful, and the earth bears fruit for the thankless. In this way the creatures were made subject to vanity, and not willingly.
For if it had depended on their will, they would not have been subject to the unworthy. Rather, it was because of him who subjected them in hope (the text reads "who did not subject" [?]);
"for the creatures themselves," he says, "will also be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the Son of God."
But if the creatures are set free at that time, will the Son then come into bondage?
Examine the Scriptures, and do not slander. Examine them, and do not search aimlessly. Examine them, believe, and do not dispute.
Where did you learn to say, “Did the Son exist before he was begotten, or did he not?” Where did you learn that begetting and making are the same?
Did Peter teach you this, or did Paul expound it, or did the Life-giver hand it down? Read the Scriptures.

You do not even stand by what you say. For when you ask, “Did he exist before he was begotten, or did he not?” you are already speaking falsely, because what you ask about is not what you acknowledge.

First confess that the Son was begotten, and then you may ask about "was" and "was not." Look, you deny the realities themselves and make the words [?]. If you do not grant him begetting, why would you demand an inquiry on that basis?

"Did the Son exist," he says, "and was he begotten, if he did not exist?" First grant me that he was begotten. First put your seal to a deed stating that he was begotten, and then inquire into the how. Look, you deny the nature, and yet you cast the words into searching and inquiry. You say that making and begetting are the same.
To me too they are not the same unless the order of the two is first made clear, and then our minds may agree. For if I should say that looking and seeing are the same, I would be saying one thing;
but if I say that hearing and seeing are the same, then I would seem to have given to the ears what belonged to the eyes.
And where did you learn that making and begetting are the same for God?

If you confessed him as begotten and made, then you would be right to say that it is the same. But if you never confess the begotten one, how can you consider begetting and making the same? You would be found not only bringing in empty words but entirely devoid of the truth.
Now we must learn why the heretic contrives to say that making and begetting are the same. "For God," he says, "is a simple and diffuse essence, and not as we are;
for we beget with some members and work with others: we beget with the generative members and work with the hands."
God is not like that, but is simple and diffuse, and without form. In the same way that he begets, he also makes.
And now, since you promise to show the conditions of invisible things, you who are puffed up with unseemly cleverness,

I will show you from these visible things that by the same manner by which works are done... Take the visible hands as an example, so that through visible things the showing [?] of the invisible may also come into view.
For whatever is done by one and the same hand is not called one and the same work, nor does it display one and the same activity.
For example: with this one and the same hand I built and demolished. Are the two the same?

For they also say, "We beget in one way and act in another way." I say the same thing in the same way: we build and we demolish with the same hand; we strike and we smooth with the same hand; we push, we throw down, and we raise up the fallen with the same hand;
and we count and undo the count [?] with the same hand. Now then, are building and demolishing the same thing?
Or striking and smoothing, and the others one by one?
Are these not the words of fools and unsuitable fables? Would Paul's thoughts not groan at this? And would Peter not be angry at mixing such words into the teaching?

Have you denied Christ, and do you learn from others? Have you not heard [?] the one who said, "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, I too will deny him"? For very many times I confess Christ, yet I am ashamed of his words.

just as you yourself would suffer [?]. When you come to discourses on theology and hear the name of the Father and of the Son, you are ashamed of the words, and you say things like this: "Did the impassible one really beget? Did he beget at all?

And if it is so, then it was by flowing out and by division." Do you see that you are ashamed of the words? It is to such people that he speaks the saying, "Whoever is ashamed of my words, I too will deny him."
Oh, the folly! They became hunters of words alone, and not true investigators of realities. Vanity, guilty before the Lord, has ruined and corrupted everything.

What I have said many times I will say now as well: the founders and leaders of the heresies are known, and the holy Church has never accepted heretical teaching. If you can ever recall a name like this that became the leader of the Church's religion, you must bring it forward. But I know that you cannot show who brought forth this sect,
which you call a sect, though it is not a sect but the truth,
which the apostles themselves preached from the beginning. After them, the Council of Nicaea confirmed the same thing,

so that it would be clear that this was the faith of the whole world and of all the earth. Of all the great multitude of bishops gathered in one place, only seven bishops did not agree, and they were thrown out as exiles and rejects.
And the whole world agreed, because they were of the mixture seasoned by the apostles.
And see these wonders: the whole new world resembled the Old Testament, just as there Abraham, who had greater faith, armed himself
with his three hundred and eighteen servants born in his household, and routed five kings of the Assyrians who had come against the land of the Palestinians.
Following the same pattern and number, Christ also gathered to himself, to make war against the heretics,
three hundred and eighteen bishops. Abraham had three hundred and eighteen servants born in his house,
and he went out against the foreigners. Although he also had many other servants bought with silver, he showed the loyalty of the servants born in his house.

Likewise, Christ did not gather everyone together indiscriminately, but those born in the household of the faith. And they proclaimed the true one from the true one, the living one from the living one, the light from the light.

What gap is there between the light and what you consider light [?]? What difference is there between the life and life? What dissimilarity is there between the truth and truth? And what is more remarkable still: the Father is called light.
John says, "God is light"; and of the Son he says, with an addition, "He was the true light."

The Father is called simply "light" because of [?], and because the heretics have dared to band together against the divinity of the Son and reduce him to a man. Yet whoever dares to act against the Son [?] brings the insult down on the Father.
Even so, the Scriptures reveal what is plain in clear words and make what is doubtful secure with the truth. The Father is called light without any addition,

because the proclamation alone is enough to make it known. The Son is also called light. So that you would not suppose that the Father is the spiritual and real light while the Son is some visible and counterfeit light, Scripture secures the statement with the addition: "He was," it says, "the true light."

Again, someone might say that the Father and the Son are like the sun and the moon: both are lights, but one is a great light and the other a small one, so the Father would be some great light and the Son a small one. To prevent this, Isaiah goes ahead beforehand and sets it right.
“Land of Zebulun,” he says, “and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the river Jordan: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.”
If the Father is called a great light, behold, the Son too is named a great light. Great is the one who begets, and great is the one begotten; great is the root, and great is the fruit.
Great is the light, and great is the radiance of the light. I recognize no great and small there, but only the great. I know the Trinity as united.
The Father is great, as the prophet Jeremiah says: "You, God, are great and everlasting." And Paul says of the Son,
if we await the blessed hope and the appearing of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ. And David says:
“Great is the Lord, and great is his power.” Surely he is not one thing and his power another? And the apostle testifies that the Son is his power: “Christ,” he says, “is the power of God.”
Again the prophet says, “Great is our Lord,” as though to say that the Father is great, and his power—the Holy Spirit—is great.
As the giver of life said to the apostles: “Stay and remain in Jerusalem until you receive power from on high.”

But see how cunningly the opponents argue. This, they say, is a power that distributes the greatness of the promises, and nowhere is it written that the Spirit is God, only that it is the pledge of the inheritance. Now pay attention:
a pledge is some part of the gift, and not the whole gift; it is a part taken from the whole.
It is written, they say, in the Apostle: "You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance."
"Do you see," they say, "that it is a gift and not God?"
Now, if you find that the Father too is called a portion and an inheritance, will you follow the words there too, rather than their meaning?
For both the inheritance and the portion are gifts from the giver, and not the one who gives the inheritance himself.
And if calling the Holy Spirit a pledge causes you to stumble, then when you hear that the Father too is a portion of the inheritance, will you direct your blasphemy against him as well?
Pay close attention. He did not say "inheritance" but "part of the inheritance."
And David testifies: "The Lord," he says, "is the portion of my inheritance."

So then, just as the Lord is the portion of the inheritance, so also the Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance. If calling the Father "the portion of the inheritance" makes him lesser, then calling the Spirit "the pledge of the inheritance" makes him lesser too. And in another place David says: "The Lord is my portion in the land of the living."
A portion is some part of a thing, and not the entire whole. Now if you are a hunter of words and not an examiner of meanings, then nothing will stop you from blaspheming God

whom you think you are glorifying. "The Lord," he says, "is the portion of my inheritance"; and "My portion is the Lord in the land of the living." If you ask why the whole Power should be called portion and inheritance, must it be explained?
For we worship God of our own free will, and one person has taken pleasure in foolishness, and another has fallen; he becomes the portion of the believers who choose him.

It is something like this: "Let the Levites," he says, "have no portion of land, for the Lord is their portion," whom they chose. And the prophet makes it clear that he chose God of his own will and not under compulsion: "The Lord," he says, "is my portion."
If God loses nothing of his divinity when he is called a portion, likewise the Holy Spirit loses nothing of his divinity when he is called a pledge.
Let us henceforth cast aside the [?] confusion and accept the apostolic faith.

How long will you set up scales and weigh the divine words? You have your thoughts in your mind like scales; then weigh the gifts of the Savior. Consider which belong to the flesh and which to the divinity,
which to his dignity and which to the dispensation, so that it may not be said of you too: "The balances of Canaan are in his hand, balances of injustice,"

and so that the other saying may not fit you: "The sons of men are vain; they sin with the balances." You hold the beam of the scales, and you distort the just balance. Be careful with the scale-pans of the Life-giver; pay attention and look closely.
"I and my Father," he says, "are one." Now where is the inequality? Look at the scale-pans of the divine word.
"He who has seen me," he says, "has seen my Father." So where is the side that sinks down, or the one that rises up?
See the Father who sets free, the Son who sets free, and the Spirit who sets free. “Unless the Son sets you free,” he says, “you are slaves.”
And Paul says, “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set us free.” If the Father sets free, and the Son sets free, and the Spirit sets free.
But may all of us be freed from the yoke of sins, escape the yoke of the heretics, uphold the steadfast faith, and give glory to the Holy Trinity forever.
